blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.text:
Homeostasis

  • The function of the organs/organ systems in our body must be co-ordinated
Co-Ordination

  • The process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another.
Neural & Endocrine System

  • Jointly coordinate and integrate all the activities of the organs so that they function in a synchronised fashion

blocks.title: Neural System
blocks.text:
• Composed of highly specialised cells = Neurons →Detect, receive & transmit different kinds of stimuli.
  • Lower invertebrates = very simple neural organisation e.g. Hydra = composed of a network of neurons.
  • Insects = Better organised neural system, Brain is present along with a numbers of ganglia & neural tissue
  • Vertebrates : More developed neural system than invertebrates

blocks.title: Question. 1
blocks.question:
Which system provides an organised network of point to point connection :-

(1) Integrated system

(2) Neuro-endocrine system

(3) Endocrine system

(4) Nervous system
blocks.answer:
Answer:4

Explanation:

The nervous system provides an organized network of point-to-point connections through neurons, which transmit electrical signals between different parts of the body. This system ensures fast and precise communication, enabling responses to stimuli within milliseconds.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
Which statement is correct regarding neuron?

(1) Neuron is composed of 4 parts containing cell body, dendrite, axon & telodendria

(2) Nissl's granules are found in both cell body & axon

(3) Impulse are divided into apolar, bipolar & multipolar

(4) Dendrites transmit impulse toward the cell body while axon transmit impulse away from the body
blocks.answer:
The correct statement is:

(4) Dendrites transmit impulses toward the cell body, while the axon transmits impulses away from the cell body.

Explanation:

  • (1) Incorrect: A neuron is composed of three main parts: the cell body (soma), dendrites, and the axon. Telodendria are terminal branches of the axon but are not considered a separate part.
  • (2) Incorrect: Nissl's granules (ribosome-studded rough endoplasmic reticulum) are found in the cell body and dendrites, but not in the axon.
  • (3) Incorrect: Neurons are classified based on the number of processes into unipolar, bipolar, and multipolar neurons, not "apolar."
  • (4) Correct: Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body, and the axon carries impulses away from the cell body.
options: (1) Neuron is composed of 4 parts containing cell body, dendrite, axon & telodendria
(2) Nissl's granules are found in both cell body & axon
(3) Impulse are divided into apolar, bipolar & multipolar
(4) Dendrites transmit impulse toward the cell body while axon transmit impulse away from the body
blocks.prompt: Which statement is correct regarding neuron?

blocks.title: Question-2
blocks.question:
Velocity of nerve impulse is more in :-

(1) Unmyelinated axons

(2) Continuous myelinated axon

(3) Discontinuous myelinated axons

(4) In dendron and cyton
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is:

(3) Discontinuous myelinated axons

Explanation:

  • Unmyelinated axons (1): The velocity of nerve impulses is slower because the signal travels continuously along the entire length of the axon.
  • Continuous myelinated axon (2): This is not a standard term because myelination inherently creates gaps (nodes of Ranvier), making axonal conduction discontinuous.
  • Discontinuous myelinated axons (3): In myelinated axons, the myelin sheath insulates the axon, and nerve impulses "jump" between the nodes of Ranvier (gaps in the myelin sheath). This process, called saltatory conduction, significantly increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission.
  • Dendron and cyton (4): Impulse transmission in dendrites (dendron) and the cell body (cyton) is not specialized for high-speed conduction like in axons.
Thus, discontinuous myelinated axons allow the fastest transmission of nerve impulses.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing Depolarization and Repolarization: It's important to remember that depolarization is the phase where the membrane potential becomes less negative (more positive), while repolarization is the phase where it returns to its resting potential.
    • Misunderstanding the role of Ion Channels: Grasp the concept of ion channels and how they regulate the movement of ions across the cell membrane.
    • Forgetting the Importance of the Sodium-Potassium Pump: This pump is crucial for maintaining the resting membrane potential and restoring ion gradients after an action potential.

Additional Tips:

• Break Down the Process: Focus on one step at a time, starting with the resting membrane potential and then moving on to depolarization, repolarization, and hyperpolarization.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
During the transmission of nerve impulse through a nerve fibre, the potential on the inner side of the plasma membrane has which type of electric charge?

(1) First positive, then negative and continue to be negative

(2) First negative, then positive and continue to be positive

(3) First positive, then negative and again back to positive

(4) First negative, then positive and again back to negative
blocks.answer:
Answer:4

Explanation:

During the transmission of a nerve impulse:

  • Resting State: (Negative)
  • Depolarization: (Positive)
  • Repolarization: (Negative)
  • Hyperpolarization and Return to Resting State: (Negative)
options: (1) First positive, then negative and continue to be negative
(2) First negative, then positive and continue to be positive
(3) First positive, then negative and again back to positive
(4) First negative, then positive and again back to negative
blocks.prompt: During the transmission of nerve impulse through a nerve fibre, the potential on the inner side of the plasma membrane has which type of electric charge?

blocks.title: Types of Neurotransmitters
blocks.text: Types of Neurotransmitters

rows: pre- and post-synaptic neurons physically separated by fluid filled synaptic cleft.
Close proximity joined by Gap junctions

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles: These vesicles fuse with the pre-synaptic membrane to release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft.
  • The synaptic cleft is a narrow gap between neurons: Neurotransmitters diffuse across this gap to reach the post-synaptic membrane.
  • Neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors: This binding triggers a response in the post-synaptic neuron.
• Synaptic transmission is a chemical process: It involves the release and binding of neurotransmitters, unlike the electrical transmission within a neuron.

blocks.title: Mid Brain
blocks.text:
Mid Brain

  • Receives and integrates visual, tactile and auditory inputs.
  • Located between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons.
Corpora quadrigemina

  • Consists of 4 round swellings (lobes) on dorsal portion of mid brain.
Cerebral aqueduct

  • Canal passes through midbrain
Brainstem

  • Mid brain + Pons + Medulla oblongata

blocks.text:

• Lobes and Their Functions
• Forgetting which lobe does what:

Frontal lobe: Thinking, planning, voluntary actions.

Parietal lobe: Sensory processing.

Occipital lobe: Vision.

Temporal lobe: Hearing and memory.

blocks.title: Distribution of Grey and White Matter
Autonomic Nervous System
blocks.text:
• Regulates involuntary functions of internal organs
  • Controls: Heart rate,Digestion,Respiration,Blood pressure,Body temperature,Pupil dilation,Salivation,Bladder control etc.

rows: Increases heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate
Decreases heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Mnemonic for Grey and White Matter: "Grey Matters, White Wires." Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies, while white matter contains myelinated axons (the "wires" that transmit information).
  • Grey Matter: Contains neuron cell bodies and is responsible for processing information.
  • White Matter: Contains myelinated axons and is responsible for transmitting information between different brain regions.
• Gyri and Sulci: These folds increase the surface area of the cerebral cortex, allowing for more neurons and connections.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
The parts of human brain that helps in regulation of sexual behaviour, expression of excitement, pleasure, rage, fear etc. are

(1) Corpora quadrigemina & hippocampus

(2) Brain stem & epithalamus

(3) Corpus callosum and thalamus

(4) Limbic system & hypothalamus
blocks.answer:
Answer- 4

Explanation:

  • The limbic system (including the amygdala, hippocampus, and cingulate gyrus) is responsible for emotions like pleasure, fear, rage, and excitement.
  • The hypothalamus plays a key role in regulating sexual behavior, pleasure, and autonomic functions by controlling hormone release from the pituitary gland.

blocks.title: Question.2
blocks.question:
Stimulation of sympathetic nervous system causes :-

(1) Constriction of blood vessels and high blood pressure

(2) Dilation of bronchi & pupil

(3) Erection of hair

(4) All of the above
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is: 4
Explanation:

The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is part of the autonomic nervous system, which prepares the body for "fight or flight" responses. Stimulation of the SNS causes all of these following effects.
options: (1) Constriction of blood vessels and high blood pressure
blocks.prompt: Stimulation of sympathetic nervous system causes :-

blocks.title: Question.3
blocks.question:
You are watching a horror movie and you notice your heart is beating fast and mouth is dry. It is because of -

(1) Fight and flight response

(2) Autonomic nervous system

(3) Sympathetic nervous system

(4) Both (1) and (3)
blocks.answer:
The correct answer is: 4
Explanation:

  • Fight and flight response: This is the body's natural reaction to stress, fear, or danger, preparing it to either confront or escape the threat. Watching a horror movie can trigger this response due to the fear it induces.
